30 May 1950
Anand, Gujarat, India

Sadguru Nirgundas Swami passes away to Akshardham

Nirgundas Swami was a pioneer in the history of BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha. He surrendered his genius, personality and standing at the feet of Shastriji Maharaj, who he humbly served until his last breath. 

In a letter dated 28 July 1949 to the politician Gulzarilal Nanda, Nirgundas Swami proclaims, “Shastriji Maharaj was never influenced by anyone and was able to control such free-willed people as me.” 

Moreover, he wrote in his personal journal: “No one had the courage to tell me to wear saffron [to become a sadhu], but Shastriji Maharaj did. He told me that my intellect, knowledge, and ability would shine more in saffron than in white. These words touched me and I became a sadhu.”

Such was Nirgundas Swami’s respect for Shastriji Maharaj, he would carry out any command given by his guru to earn his rajipo.

Inspired by Gunatitanand Swami’s vision of Satsang being spread to all corners of the Earth and by Shastriji Maharaj’s words, Nirgundas Swami began writing of the greatness of Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj and Shastriji Maharaj in a stream of letters to Africa, where Harmanbhai and Maganbhai, two devotees, had established Satsang. Nirgundas Swami’s letters were not just a few pages long, but were sometimes up to a hundred pages in length! Moreover, his letters were organised, well-written, point-to-point, clear, and faithful to the principles of the Vachanamrut and other scriptures of the Sampraday.

Shastriji Maharaj would often speak of the pivotal role played by Nirgundas Swami in propagating the Akshar-Purushottam upasana through vicharan, letters and katha.

Today is World Environment Day, a moment to reflect not just on the state of our planet, but on the lives of those who honour it every single day through their actions, their choices, and their love. 

One such person is our very own guru, Mahant Swami Maharaj.

From the very beginning, Mahant Swami Maharaj’s bond with nature has been intimate and reverent. As a young man, he studied agriculture. In every major festival of BAPS, he was given the responsibility of landscaping. While others may see trees and nature as decoration, he saw them as something to revere and care for. He would plant each sapling with care and even talk to the plants. He would address them as muktas. This has been seen by many eyewitnesses of his seva. He would speak to the plants and lovingly encourage them to grow. Science today tells us that such words, such intention, can help plants thrive.

As the spiritual leader of BAPS, Mahant Swami Maharaj continues to inspire and guide countless environmental initiatives around the world. From promoting sustainable temple construction to initiating large-scale water relief projects during droughts, and championing recycling and waste reduction efforts, his vision extends across the global BAPS community. Yet these actions are not mere compliance with modern trends; they flow from his own deep ethic of respect, responsibility, and harmony with nature.

Even now, at 92, his care for the environment is lived out in the smallest of gestures. 
- He never lets the tap run when brushing his teeth; he fills a small vessel and uses only what is needed. 
- Just last year, he waited patiently for an ant to climb out of a sink before letting the water flow. 
- In Melbourne, a few horses were grazing outside his residence. He had been resting, but upon waking, his very first question was whether the horses had been fed and cared for. 

At 92. Imagine, then, the decades before, how many animals he must have noticed, how many trees he must have planted, how many small, unseen acts of compassion he must have carried out. 

For Mahant Swami Maharaj, to love God is to love all that God has made.

Following his 7-year van vicharan and 10 long months in Loj, 19-year-old Nilkanth Varni first meets Guru Ramanand Swami in the village of Piplana on 18 June 1800.

Ramanand Swami repeated what he had been saying for many years: “I am only a drumbeater, but the real actor is this brahmachari Nilkanth.”

Four months later, in Piplana, on 28 October 1800 (Kartak sud 11), he gave bhagvati diksha to Nilkanth and named him Sahajanand Swami and Narayanmuni.

Nishkulanand Swami describes this meeting in Piplana in prakran 44 of the Bhaktachintamani:

Param hitkārī bahunāmī, dīṭhā sinhāsan par swāmī. 25
Tene dekhīne pāmyā ānand, tyāre uṭhyā Swāmī Rāmānand;
Karyā Nīlkanṭhe danḍavat, tene uṭhāḍyā swāmīe tarat. 26
Preme maḷīne besāryā pās, karī bījānī bahu āsavās;
Jevā kahyātā sādhue maḷī, tevā dīṭhā chhe Varṇīe vaḷī. 27
Pāmyā paramānand sukh bhārī, āvyā harṣhanā nayaṇe vāri;
Thayā brahmachārī romānchite, joī rahyā sāmu bahu prītye. 28
Tem joī rahyā swāmī hete, ek mīṭe maṭakā rahite;

Seated (left to right)

1. Pujya Arun Bhagat (Pujya Ishwarcharandas Swami)

2. Pujya Narayan Bhagat (Pujya Viveksagardas Swami)

3. Pujya Niranjan Bhagat (Pujya Siddheshwardas Swami)

Standing (left to right)

2. Pujya Madhu Bhagat

12 July 1991
Opening of Cultural Festival of India by Pramukh Swami Maharaj in Edison, New Jersey

Held from 12 July to 11 August 1991, the Cultural Festival of India (CFI) was a 31-day celebration held on the grounds of the Middlesex County College in Edison, New Jersey. 

This festival was an amazing depiction of Indian talent and art in which craftsmen created beautiful mandirs, gates, and artifacts featuring intricate carvings. The stunning Indian villages, charming dances, enchanting musical performances by maestros, and awe-inspiring exhibitions shared India’s majestic culture with North America. 

The festival’s three exhibitions displayed moral stories highlighting universal values of family harmony, compassion, and love.

CFI featured 4 magnificent mandirs and 5 beautiful archways, with 40 acres of landscaped gardens and fountains. 

Daily, over 150 children and youths performed 26 different types of traditional Indian folk dance from various parts of India, such as Bhangra from Punjab, Teratali from Rajasthan, and Raas-Garba from Gujarat. People entered the fairgrounds eager to experience the sights and sounds of India.

Visitors also left with a taste of India as this festival had 20 food stalls, each of which offered exquisite Indian delicacies. 

CFI shared and celebrated India’s culture with over 1.2 million visitors from North America and the world.

Festival Highlights:

1.2 million visitors from around the world.
Middlesex County came to be known as ‘Little India.’
Over 150 children and youths performed 26 different folk dances and theatrical performances daily.
A traditional Indian village, complete with bazaars, fairs, and traditional entertainment, was recreated.
Computer and multimedia booths gave an interactive peek at India’s heritage.
2,100 volunteers dedicated tens of thousands of volunteer hours.
3 cultural exhibits, ‘India – A Cultural Millionaire,’ ‘In the Joy of Others Lies our Own,’ and ‘Beautiful Borderless World,’ depicted lessons from India’s rich heritage.
40 acres of lush gardens and fountains adorned the festival grounds.

Selected discourses of Bhagwan Swaminarayan delivered between 1819 and 1829 have been compiled in the Vachanamrut, which contains a total of 273 discourses.

Narrated on 25 July 1829, the last recorded Vachanamrut was 'Gadhada III 39: Vishalyakaraṇī Aushadhinu'.

In the conclusion of this final Vachanamrut, Bhagwan Swaminarayan says:
▪️"It is the principle of all of the scriptures that one should eradicate māyā and develop love for God."
▪️ “A devotee of God requires the strength of two things: ātmā-realization and the greatness of God."
▪️"I deliver these discourses to you not from any imagination of my mind, nor to display any sort of aptitude. I have experienced all that I have spoken about. In fact, I speak in accordance to what I practice."

It was also the final Vachanamrut that was read to Yogiji Maharaj. On the early morning of 16 January 1971, a week before he passed away to Akshardham, Yogiji Maharaj asked for the Vachanamrut to be read. The sevak read this Vachanamut. After this, until his passing, Yogiji Maharaj was not able to listen to the Vachanamrut again.

20 July 1985 became a part of BAPS history as Queens Park Rangers Stadium witnessed the first ever Suvarna Mahotsav held to honour Pramukh Swami Maharaj. 

The volunteers had worked hard for several months in planning and setting up the festival, and for them this was going to be the ultimate experience.

However, at Swamishri’s wish, they stayed at the Cultural Festival of India grounds at Alexandra Park to run the exhibitions, food stalls, and other departments. 

The moment of supreme joy arrived at QPR Stadium. Swamishri had been honoured and thousands cheered his name and echoed cries of jubilation.

When the celebrations were over, a sadhu asked Swamishri, “What were you thinking while being weighed?” “I was thinking about the yuvaks who were doing seva back at Ally Pally.”

Swamishri’s response was instant and thought-provoking. It is impossible to think of others while one is being showered with such honour and praise.

A few days later, on 5 August, Swamishri, out of sheer compassion, arranged for a special festival for the volunteers.

The vibrations from the voices of the sadhus and parshads singing could be felt in each and every person's heart, as Swamishri plucked people from the crowd to join in a dance at the end of the special Suvarna Mahotsav programme arranged exclusively for the volunteers.

The few precious seconds previously witnessed at QPR Stadium when Swamishri had danced before departing, were brought back again. This time, his beloved volunteers were much closer and, for them, Swamishri danced a little longer. 

Unbelievable scenes of jubilation, unimaginable atmosphere and bliss... 

This was how Swamishri rewarded those volunteers who had stayed back to serve at the CFI grounds at Alexandra Park.

Bapa,
 
Today was a day we want to forget but that we never will.
Heartache, wrenching pain, and an endless flow of tears.
Wails of pain, anguish and sorrow heard in every corner. 
Grief is the price of love is what we realised on that fateful day.

Today, we were all the same. 
Age, gender, nationality, sadhu, householder - nothing mattered.
We were sat, for hours, in the scorching heat, as one family. 
Your family.
You had said 'BAPS Ek Parivar' many times, but on that day, we felt it like never before.
Our hearts and minds united by our love, and grief, for you.

Today, we welcomed you for the final time.
For decades, your arrivals were always the most memorable. Moments that filled our hearts with elation. Today, however, our hearts were empty. Void. Numb.
You taught us to perform bhakti and adorned our lives with puja, thal, arti.
Today was the last arti we would offer to you.

Today, we would see your mesmerising face for the last time.
Your beautiful, innocent face would light up our lives with joy.
But today was different. There was only pain.
The final time this earth was graced with the presence of your body... 
The smile that mesmerised millions...
The arms that helped thousands...
The hands that blessed countless...
The legs that walked from house to house...
All to give to joy to others.

Today, a day we would never imagine.
You were invincible. You were the Bapa that would always be there.
You were the Bapa we were born with. Bapa that was always a ‘given' in life.
For those four days you were still before our eyes, with us.
But today, you – the almighty, the powerful, the Bapa that would be there forever – were suddenly engulfed by flames.

Today, we realised how deep your devotion was.
Guru and God were the focus throughout your life.
In your final seconds, you had your beloved Thakorji on your chest.
And the murti of your guru in your presence.
Today, even after you have breathed your last, your devotion remains eternal.

18 August 1897
Shravan vad 6
Junagadh, India

Bhagatji Maharaj welcomed with a grand reception at Junagadh

Since his exile from the Satsang - imposed by the authorities in Vadtal for propagating the glory of Gunatitanand Swami - Bhagatji Maharaj had not visited Junagadh. 

Over 30 years had passed, yet Bhagatji Maharaj did not go to Junagadh due to opposition and the absence of Acharya Maharaj’s orders. Shastri Yagnapurushdasji, however, decided to accord a grand reception to Bhagatji at the very place where he had been insulted.

In VS 1953 (1897 CE), he persuaded Acharya Viharilalji Maharaj to invite Bhagatji on the occasion of the Janmashtami festival to be celebrated in Junagadh.

Bhagatji Maharaj arrived in Junagadh two days prior to the festival. He was received along with Acharya Maharaj at Junagadh railway station with traditional fanfare. Like Acharya Maharaj, Bhagatji Maharaj and his disciples were driven in a decorated carriage. Special arrangements were made at the mandir to make their stay comfortable. Yagnapurushdasji was assisted by Kothari Jibhai of Junagadh in making these arrangements for Bhagatji.

The news of Bhagatji’s arrival in Junagadh spread all over the city. All the Nagar devotees came to the mandir for Bhagatji’s darshan. Here, he met senior sadhus such as Balmukunddasji and Jaga Bhagat, who had sincerely served Aksharbrahma Gunatitanand Swami. For many days, these great stalwarts of the Gunatit Gnan came together to engage in discourses and scriptural discussions to extol the glory of Akshar and Purushottam.

Bhagatji's disciples had sponsored the meals on the day after Janmashtami at Junagadh Mandir where he served the sadhus and devotees most affectionately.

It was during this time in Junagadh that the Akshar-Purushottam philosophy could be freely discussed. It was also during this time that Jaga Bhakta of Junagadh inspired Shastriji Maharaj to install the murtis of Akshar-Purushottam in the central shrine of a shikharbaddh mandir. 

Amazingly, exactly 98 years to the day that this event unfolded in Junagadh, Pramukh Swami Maharaj commenced the six-day Mandir Mahotsav in London on 18 August 1995 to mark the opening of the first Akshar-Purushottam shikharbaddh mandir outside India.

21 August 1799 
Shravan vad 6 
Loj, India

After his epic 2,610 days (7 years, 1 month and 24 days) of pilgrimage throughout India, covering over 12,000 kilometres, Nilkanth Varni arrived in Loj.

Nilkanth bathed in the stepwell and retired into a meditative posture beneath a sprawling banyan tree nearby. 

Sukhanand Swami from Ramanand Swami’s ashram came to fill his pot from the stepwell.

Upon seeing the gentle, teenage yogi, he, too, was mesmerised. He came and stood before Nilkanth, waiting for him to open his eyes.

Sukhanand Swami asked: “Brahmachariji, where do you come from? What is your name? Who are your parents? Why have you renounced your home? And who is your guru?” 

“Sadhuram! A renunciant has no caste, country, or relatives. One who redeems from worldly bondage is a true parent or guru! I am in search of such a guru,” Nilkanth replied softly.

Nilkanth Varni then proceeded to the ashram in Loj to meet Muktanand Swami. Nilkanth revealed to Muktanand Swami: “My mind is at peace in your ashram. The sadhus here are of a peaceful disposition.” 

“You may ask freely whatever questions you have,” Muktanand Swami requested.

Nilkanth then posed the five questions he had been asking throughout his travels. Muktanand Swami satisfactorily elaborated upon the natures of jiva, ishwar, maya, Brahma and Parabrahma. Nilkanth was satisfied with the answers and decided to stay at the ashram for the darshan of guru Ramanand Swami.

On the Occasion of Paris Mandir Murti Pratishtha

English Translation
Dearest Yogi Bapa,

​You used to express the vision that Satsang would spread around the world. When you used to name various countries, no one could believe it. But today, as the consecration of this mandir in Paris has taken place and its glory resounds, everyone is filled with conviction.

​In 1970, when you instructed Pramukh Swami and me to set foot on the soil of Paris, it was truly you who resided within us, setting foot here and sowing the seeds of Satsang. You made us an instrument and granted us the opportunity to serve.

​Everyone keeps marvelling that 'you are travelling at the age of 93', but Bapa, spiritual LOVE has no limits. We live for you. Fulfilling your vision is our life and our bhakti. ​Even that is accomplished only through your divine strength.

​Whoever has rendered service (seva) for this mandir, we offer all of that today at your holy feet.

​O Yogi Bapa! Please accept our humble offering (anjali).

​Your servant,

Sadhu Keshavjivandas

8 September 1981

Cholecystectomy operation to remove gall bladder performed on Pramukh Swami Maharaj at Cumballa Hill Hospital, Mumbai, by Dr A.R. Patel. 

The gall bladder was removed due to multiple gallstones and had been causing health issues for some time. Despite the difficulties, Swamishri's vicharan had continued unabated, and he had resisted doctors' recommendations to have the surgery done in 1980, instead preferring to wait until the bicentenary celebrations of Bhagwan Swaminarayan were complete.

It was a major operation in those days - nowadays it can be simply removed by keyhole laparoscopic surgery - requiring many days in hospital post-operation. After resting and recuperating in Mumbai, Swamishri resumed his vicharan.

Soon after the gall bladder operation, Swamishri was in Gondal. 

One day, after Swamishri took breakfast, a balak named Chandrakant came rushing. He asked Swamishri in childish prattle, “Bapa, where is your operation scar?” He had once heard his parents talking about the operation.

The devotees who saw the child were quite surprised with the balak's request. Swamishri, however, casually lifted his upper cloth (gatariyu) and showed him the scar. He said to the balak, “Here, run your hand on it so that it heals soon.” Innocently, Chandrakant ran his hand on the scar. Swamishri then remarked, “Now it will heal quickly."

Such was Swamishri's affectionate nature.

Prasang on Swamishri's devotion:
Following his cataract operation, Pramukh Swami was recovering in a room at the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary. His eyes were bandaged shut and so he called out and asked as to who was present. A local youth was sitting in the room and asked Swami what he needed. Since it was the evening, Swami asked him to recite the cheshta. At this point, Swami instructed the youth to open his own (Swami’s) puja, take out the ‘Nityavidhi’ and had him recite the cheshta from the book. 28 September 1784

Aksharbrahma Gunatitanand Swami is born as Mulji Sharma in Bhadra on the auspicious day of Sharad Purnima. 

Gunatitanand Swami was the first spiritual successor of Bhagwan Swaminarayan. He was revealed by Bhagwan Swaminarayan to be Aksharbrahma, the perfectly enlightened ideal devotee and the closest entity to God, glorified in the Vedas, Upanishads, Bhagwad Gita, and many other Hindu shastras. 

Aksharbrahma Gunatitanand Swami extolled Bhagwan Swaminarayan’s true glory as Parabrahma Purushottam Narayan through his profound saintliness, matchless wisdom, inspiring discourses, and constant communion with God. His discipline, devotion, and service were exemplary, inspiring all who came into his contact. 

As Aksharbrahma, he forever remains manifest on Earth as the enlightened guru, helping aspirants attain moksha.

This remarkable painting, created in 1860, is now over 165 years old and stands as one of the earliest known visual representations of Gunatitanand Swami Maharaj. At the time, he was around 75 years old, radiating divine serenity and spiritual strength — qualities beautifully captured in this historic artwork. 

What makes this painting even more extraordinary is that it is currently the only known and most accurate depiction of Gunatitanand Swami Maharaj. It not only preserves his physical appearance, but also serves as a timeless tribute to his profound wisdom, selfless service, and eternal presence as Akshar, the divine abode of Bhagwan Swaminarayan. 

This sacred image continues to inspire generations of devotees, offering a rare and invaluable glimpse into the divine past.

Afterwards, Mahant Swami Maharaj and senior swamis went to the banks of the river to inaugurate the Akshar and Brahma Kunds – built for relatives to ritually bathe after dispersing the ashes of their kin.
